thread.title: Qualcomm Is Yielding 4.3% But Licensing Disputes Need To Be Resolved - Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM)

author: Dividend Power
title: Qualcomm Is Yielding 4.3% But Licensing Disputes Need To Be Resolved - Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM)
text:
Overview I have focused my articles and analyses mostly on industrial, consumer staples, and utility sectors to date with some exceptions. But my general theme has been to write about stocks with decent income and a growing dividend over time with the potential for capital appreciation. In this article, I discuss Qualcomm Inc. ( QCOM ) which has a dividend yield > 4%, a growing dividend and is undervalued based on PE ratio relative to the S&P 500. But despite this, I am not a buyer of Qualcomm due to its ongoing legal disputes with the FTC and regulators in other countries, and Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) and other companies over licensing and royalty practices.
Dividend Power’s Investment Process As a small investor, one is always seeking suitable entry points or to add to a position for stocks that generate decent income but have a safe yield. Historically, tech stocks were not thought of as a source of income or dividend growth. But that has changed and there exist now tech stocks paying dividend yields greater than some companies in the consumer staples and utility sectors.
Tech Stocks Can Provide Decent Income
Source: dignited.com
For my Dividend Growth stock watch list, I filter with the following quantitative criteria:
Large cap stocks that have a history of increasing dividends > 10 years, A dividend yield > 3%, A payout ratio of 65% or lower, PE ratio < S&P 500’s average, and Long-term debt-to-equity (D/E) < 2. Although I have criteria to follow, they serve primarily to narrow the broader list of stocks to a smaller set of companies for further research. On a case-by-case basis, I make exceptions to the aforesaid criteria if a company meets some but not all five criteria. Qualcomm meets four of the five criteria and does not meet the D/E ratio criteria due to large share buybacks. Once I determine if the company meets my criteria then I examine both quantitative and qualitative aspects.
Qualcomm Controls Key Patents for Mobile Phones Qualcomm develops, patents, and licenses wireless technology. It is this part of the company’s business, known as Qualcomm Technology Licensing (QTL), which gives the company a moat and is Qualcomm’s strength. The company has important patents for code-division multiple access (CDMA) and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access (OFDMA) technologies in mobile phones. These technologies are used in essentially all 3G phones and most 4G phones, but the latter are backwards compatible and hence Qualcomm receives royalties on the majority of mobile phones that are sold around the world. In addition, Qualcomm has a large business designing and selling chipsets (processors) for mobile phones. Qualcomm’s flagship mobile phone technology is the Snapdragon system on a chip (SoC). This part of the company’s business is referred to as Qualcomm CDMA Technologies (QCT).
Qualcomm Snapdragon System on a Chip for Mobile Phones
Source: cnet.com
Qualcomm Has an Above Average Dividend Yield Qualcomm is interesting from the perspective of both yield and dividend growth. The current dividend yield is ~4.3%, which is greater than many consumer staples companies and some utilities, and the payout ratio is ~60%, meeting my criteria. The yield is near an all-time high, as seen in the chart below, and it is also greater than the S&P 500’s recent average yield of ~2.1%. Furthermore, the company has grown its dividend for 16 straight years with a 10-year growth rate of over 17% CAGR. However, I expect this growth rate to slow in the future and, in fact, the dividend only grew ~8.5% in the last year. But since payout ratio is already ~60% and, as we discuss below both revenue and FCF are declining, I expect that this rate will decrease further in the near future.
Qualcomm’s 10-Year Dividend Yield History
Source: Seeking Alpha
From a PE perspective, Qualcomm has PE ratio (FWD) of ~13.9 based on consensus earnings estimates that are below the S&P 500’s current PE ratio of ~19.5, making the company undervalued relative to the broader market. However, Qualcomm is overvalued on a PE ratio (FWD) basis compared to Intel Corp. ( INTC ), a major competitor in mobile wireless, which has a PE ratio (FWD) of ~10.8. One must also remember that Intel has a dominant PC processor business. In any event, starting with a $2.43 dividend in FY2018 and assuming an 8% desired return and a stable 3%-4% dividend growth gives a valuation of $48.60-$60.75, making Qualcomm’s current stock price in the range of reasonable expectations.
Revenue Growth Has Not Been Consistent The company has beaten revenue and EPS estimates for the past seven quarters. But organic revenue growth has been volatile on a YoY basis and furthermore guidance for next quarter was weak, pressuring the stock price. In addition, revenue peaked at ~$26.5B in FY2014 and has since declined to ~$22.7B in FY2018. Furthermore, Qualcomm’s licensing revenues are being impacted by the ongoing legal disputes. Qualcomm has not recorded any royalty revenue since Q3 FY2017 on sale of Apple products. The company has stated, “GAAP and Non-GAAP results have been negatively impacted by our dispute with Apple and its contract manufacturers (who are our licensees)”. Qualcomm is also being impacted by partial payment of royalty revenue from another licensee identified in the Q4 FY2018 earnings release, which is likely Huawei Technologies Co. In any case, the amount of revenue impacted was reportedly ~$1.7B in FY2017 alone, which is substantial. If the legal disputes are not resolved in Qualcomm’s favor, then royalty and licensing revenue will be lower in the future.
Notably, net income, EBITDA, and FCF are down since revenue peaked in FY2014. Net income was ~$7.97B in FY2014 and dropped to $2.47B in FY2017 and -$4.86B in FY2018 (due to a charge for the Tax Cut and Jobs Act). Simultaneously, EBITDA was $9.93B in FY2014 then decreased to $2.84B in FY2018 and FCF was $7.7B in FY2014 declining to $3.11B in FY2018. Clearly the loss of revenue from royalty payments has had a significant negative impact on Qualcomm.
Will Automotive Chip and 5G Technologies Drive Future Revenue Growth? Qualcomm has made an effort to expand in automotive chip business areas not related to mobile phones. Qualcomm tried but was not successful in acquiring NXP Semiconductors ( NXPI ), an automotive chip company, and thus Qualcomm is still primarily a mobile phone technology company. However, Qualcomm is increasing its investment and development efforts in automotive chip technologies in order to expand its product line. Along these lines, Qualcomm has introduced the company’s 3 rd Generation Snapdragon Automotive Platforms built on the Snapdragon 820A chipset. This technology permits voice controls to navigation systems with modern visual interfaces. Although Qualcomm is moving in the right direction by expanding its product line, the automotive chip market is much smaller than the mobile phone chipset market and may not be as significant a driver of revenue growth.
Qualcomm is also moving forward in 2019 with the company’s 5G mobile phone technologies, including the Snapdragon 855 chipset and X50 5G modem. The company recently announced that its 5G technologies would launch in over 30 mobile devices in 2019. However, 5G networks are still in the early stages of implementation and will likely not be an immediate revenue growth driver.
Risks Are Present Since Legal Disputes Are Not Resolved and Competition is Increasing Qualcomm has been the subject of actions and fines from regulators in China, Korea, Europe, Taiwan, and the U.S. over anticompetitive business practices and royalties. There is the risk that Qualcomm’s licensing and royalty disputes will not be resolved in the company’s favor , which would negatively impact Qualcomm’s royalty revenue stream. The main risk here is that Qualcomm receives royalties at a lower base rate instead of the full price of the phone, as was industry practice. In fact, this was the outcome in China, when in 2015 the base rate was set at 65% of the price of the phone . However, Qualcomm has recently obtained more favorable rulings in China and Germany regarding some of its patents in the company’s legal dispute, with Apple indicating that it may be somewhat successful in defending royalty revenue. But uncertainty about the legal disputes is a major concern for small investors interested in income and dividend growth until resolved.
Qualcomm’s mobile SoC technology business segment is facing increasing competition from Intel Corp. and phone manufacturers who are bringing some of this work in-house. In particular, Intel has improved its mobile chipset technologies and won some business from Apple over Qualcomm starting with the iPhone7. Additionally, Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) has used its own chipset designs for some of its Galaxy phones. I expect these trends to continue as Intel expands in the mobile phone technologies market and phone manufacturers such as Samsung and Huawei develop proprietary technologies, particularly in 5G technologies.
Debt Has Increased Another concern is Qualcomm’s use of debt for share buybacks. The company had no debt as recently as FY2014, but short-term debt increased to ~$1B and long-term debt increased to ~$15.4B at the end of FY2018. One use of this debt has been to fund share buybacks, which is not a good use of debt in my opinion. The D/E ratio at the end of FY2017 was 0.63 which meets my criteria but increased significantly to ~16.6 at the end of FY2018 due to large share repurchases and corresponding decrease in equity as seen in the chart below. However, Qualcomm’s debt is offset by ~$12.1B in cash and short-term investments at the end of FY2018 and thus the company has sufficient liquidity to meet its obligations. The cash position also provides some safety for the dividend in the event of a broader economic slowdown or if Qualcomm does not successfully resolve its legal disputes.

Final Thoughts Although Qualcomm is on my watch list, I have not yet bought a starter position mostly due to increasing competition from Intel and the company’s well-known legal disputes with regulators, Apple , and other companies over licensing and royalties. I believe that these legal issues will weigh on the company’s stock price until resolved. The possibility exists that the legal disputes will not be resolved in Qualcomm’s favor leading to lower royalty revenue. In addition, I view the company as fairly valued at the moment with some downside risk due to the uncertainty regarding the legal disputes. Hence, I am not a buyer of Qualcomm.
For readers interested in other Dividend Growth stocks that I view as a buy, I recently wrote an article at the end of 2018 entitled “ 4 Dividend Growth Stocks To Think About For The New Year ”. I have also written a recent article entitled “ Cisco is Gaining Traction ”, which I view as a buy for a dividend growth tech stock.
